# Learning goals

In this lab you will:

- simulate random variables with `sample()` and the `r` functions, and make results reproducible with `set.seed()`;
- see the law of large numbers at work;
- estimate probabilities by Monte Carlo (birthday problem, Monty Hall, a dice game) and compare with exact values;
- compare empirical and theoretical distributions;
- explore the sampling distribution of the mean and get a first look at the central limit theorem (CLT).

Work in pairs. Plan for 60–75 minutes.

# Setup

```{r}
rivers <- read.csv("data/rivers.csv")     # length_miles, 141 North American rivers
len <- rivers$length_miles
set.seed(2027)
```

`set.seed()` fixes the random numbers, so you and your partner get the same results. Change it to see how much a simulation varies.

# Monte Carlo in one idea

To estimate $P(A)$: repeat the experiment $N$ times, and compute the proportion of repetitions in which $A$ occurs. The standard error of this estimate is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/N}$.

```{r}
# P(sum of two dice is 8)? Exact value: 5/36
N <- 100000
sim <- sample(1:6, N, replace = TRUE) + sample(1:6, N, replace = TRUE)
p_hat <- mean(sim == 8)
c(estimate = p_hat, exact = 5/36, se = sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / N))
```

# Law of large numbers

The running proportion of heads converges to $1/2$.

```{r}
n <- 5000
flips <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
running <- cumsum(flips) / seq_len(n)
plot(running, type = "l", log = "x", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "number of flips (log scale)", ylab = "proportion of heads")
abline(h = 0.5, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

Repeat with several independent sequences to see that all of them settle near 0.5, whereas the early values wander:

```{r}
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, n), ylim = c(0, 1), log = "x",
     xlab = "number of flips (log scale)", ylab = "proportion of heads")
for (s in 1:8) lines(cumsum(rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)) / seq_len(n), col = s)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2)
```

The same for a continuous variable: the running mean of $U(0,1)$ draws approaches $0.5$.

```{r}
u <- runif(n)
plot(cumsum(u) / seq_len(n), type = "l", log = "x",
     xlab = "n", ylab = "running mean")
abline(h = 0.5, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

**Your turn.** Plot the running mean of 5000 draws of an exponential with rate 2 (`rexp(n, 2)`). To what value does it converge, and why?

# Birthday problem

In a group of $n$ people, what is the probability that at least two share a birthday (365 equally likely days)? The exact value is
$$
1-\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{365-i}{365}.
$$

```{r}
birthday_exact <- function(n) 1 - prod((365 - 0:(n - 1)) / 365)
birthday_sim <- function(n, N = 10000) {
  mean(replicate(N, any(duplicated(sample(1:365, n, replace = TRUE)))))
}
birthday_exact(23)
birthday_sim(23)

ns <- c(10, 20, 23, 30, 40, 50, 60)
round(rbind(exact = sapply(ns, birthday_exact),
            simulated = sapply(ns, birthday_sim)), 3)
```

```{r}
nn <- 1:80
plot(nn, sapply(nn, birthday_exact), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "group size n", ylab = "P(shared birthday)")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2)
```

**Your turn.** Find the smallest $n$ for which the exact probability exceeds $0.9$ (use `which(...)[1]`).

# Monty Hall

There are three doors, one with a car. You pick a door; the host, who knows where the car is, opens another door with a goat; you may switch to the remaining closed door.

```{r}
monty <- function(switch, N = 10000) {
  car  <- sample(1:3, N, replace = TRUE)
  pick <- sample(1:3, N, replace = TRUE)
  win <- logical(N)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    # the host opens a door that is neither the pick nor the car
    options <- setdiff(1:3, c(pick[i], car[i]))
    opened <- if (length(options) == 1) options else sample(options, 1)
    final <- if (switch) setdiff(1:3, c(pick[i], opened)) else pick[i]
    win[i] <- final == car[i]
  }
  mean(win)
}
c(stay = monty(FALSE), switch = monty(TRUE))
```

Switching wins with probability $2/3$: the first pick is right with probability $1/3$, and then switching loses; otherwise switching wins.

**Your turn.** Change the game to 4 doors (the host opens one goat door after your pick). Predict the probability of winning by switching and then simulate it. (Hint: the pick is right with probability $1/4$; switching then chooses one of the 2 other closed doors at random.)

# A dice game

Two players, A and B, each roll a die. The larger of the two rolls decides: if the largest roll is 4 or less, A wins; otherwise B wins. Is the game fair?

```{r}
simulate_game <- function() {
  roll_A <- sample(1:6, 1)
  roll_B <- sample(1:6, 1)
  largest_roll <- max(roll_A, roll_B)
  if (largest_roll <= 4) "Player A wins" else "Player B wins"
}
N <- 10000
results <- replicate(N, simulate_game())
table(results) / N
```

Exact calculation: $P(\max\le 4)=(4/6)^2=4/9\approx 0.444$. The game favours B.

```{r}
(4/6)^2
# a faster vectorised simulation
rA <- sample(1:6, 1e6, replace = TRUE); rB <- sample(1:6, 1e6, replace = TRUE)
mean(pmax(rA, rB) <= 4)
```

**Your turn.** Change the rule so that A wins when the largest roll is at most $k$. Find by computing $(k/6)^2$ the value of $k$ that makes the game closest to fair, and check by simulation.

# Empirical versus theoretical distributions

Simulate the number of heads in 10 tosses, many times, and compare with $\mathrm{Bin}(10, 0.5)$.

```{r}
x <- rbinom(10000, size = 10, prob = 0.5)
emp <- table(factor(x, levels = 0:10)) / 10000
round(rbind(empirical = emp, theoretical = dbinom(0:10, 10, 0.5)), 4)
barplot(emp, ylim = c(0, 0.3), xlab = "number of heads", ylab = "relative frequency")
points(seq(0.7, by = 1.2, length.out = 11), dbinom(0:10, 10, 0.5), pch = 19, col = "red")
```

For a continuous variable compare the histogram with the density, and the empirical cdf (`ecdf()`) with the theoretical cdf.

```{r}
y <- rexp(5000, rate = 0.5)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(y, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "grey90", border = "white", main = "histogram")
curve(dexp(x, 0.5), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(ecdf(y), main = "empirical cdf", do.points = FALSE)
curve(pexp(x, 0.5), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
c(mean(y), 1 / 0.5, var(y), 1 / 0.5^2)
```

**Inverse transform.** If $U\sim U(0,1)$ then $F^{-1}(U)$ has cdf $F$. For the exponential, $F^{-1}(u)=-\log(1-u)/\lambda$.

```{r}
u <- runif(5000)
y2 <- -log(1 - u) / 0.5
ks.test(y2, "pexp", 0.5)$p.value       # no evidence against Exp(0.5)
qqplot(y, y2); abline(0, 1, col = "red")
```

**Your turn.** Simulate 10000 values of the sum of two dice and compare the empirical pmf with the exact one, `c(1:6, 5:1)/36`.

# Sampling distribution of the mean and a CLT preview

Take the 141 river lengths as a population. They are strongly right-skewed.

```{r}
c(mu = mean(len), sigma = sqrt(mean((len - mean(len))^2)))
hist(len, breaks = 30, col = "grey90", border = "white", main = "Population", xlab = "miles")
```

Draw many samples of size $n$ and record the mean of each:

```{r}
mu <- mean(len); sigma <- sqrt(mean((len - mu)^2))
sample_means <- function(n, B = 5000) replicate(B, mean(sample(len, n, replace = TRUE)))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (n in c(2, 5, 30, 100)) {
  m <- sample_means(n)
  hist(m, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, col = "grey90", border = "white",
       main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "sample mean")
  curve(dnorm(x, mu, sigma / sqrt(n)), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The mean of the sample means is near $\mu$, their standard deviation is near $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and for large $n$ their histogram follows the normal curve, although the population is not normal.

```{r}
sapply(c(2, 5, 30, 100), function(n) {
  m <- sample_means(n)
  c(n = n, mean = mean(m), sd = sd(m), theory_sd = sigma / sqrt(n))
})
```

**Your turn.** For $n=30$, estimate $P(\bar X>700)$ by simulation and by the normal approximation, `1 - pnorm(700, mu, sigma / sqrt(30))`. Then repeat the CLT experiment with a sum of 12 dice instead of river lengths: histogram of `colSums(matrix(sample(1:6, 12 * 5000, replace = TRUE), nrow = 12))`.

# Wrap-up

Monte Carlo replaces a hard calculation by repetition. The error shrinks like $1/\sqrt N$: a hundred times more repetitions give ten times more accuracy. The CLT explains why the normal distribution is so useful for sample means, and prepares confidence intervals (Lab 03).
